source_refs.note: Chapter 16 exercise (PDF 348-349), solved: 7 MCQs keyed (no key printed), 11 short and 4 descriptive questions with model answers. Indicator theory and confirmatory salt-analysis tests are beyond the chapter and labelled so.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. While taking a reading with a burette, why it is always advisable to read the lower meniscus for the colorless liquids and the upper meniscus for the coloured liquids?

options.text: because colorless liquids have more surface tension than colored liquids
because lower meniscus does not exist for colored liquids

blocks.explanation: In a dark coloured liquid (e.g. KMnO₄ solution) the lower meniscus cannot be seen through the liquid, so the clearly visible upper meniscus is read; in a colourless liquid the lower meniscus is clear (beyond the chapter). Parallax (d) is avoided by keeping the eye level with the meniscus, whichever is read.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) is loosely worded: a coloured liquid does have a lower meniscus, but it cannot be seen through the liquid. (c) is the intended answer.

blocks.prompt: II. Why phenolphthalein indicator is more appropriate to use during the titrations which involve a strong acid and a strong base?

options.text: because it is itself weakly acidic
because the pH at the equivalence point as well as the pH over where the colour of phenolphthalein changes match each-other.
because the solution at the end of titration is acidic.
because the solution at the end of titration is basic.

blocks.explanation: An indicator is suitable when its colour-change range falls within the sharp jump of pH at the equivalence point. For strong acid–strong base the pH jumps steeply (about 3 to 11) around pH 7, covering phenolphthalein's range (about 8 to 10), so one drop changes the colour (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: III. Which cation gives a white gelatinous precipitate upon the addition of aqueous ammonia?
blocks.explanation: Al³⁺ gives a white gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)₃ that does not dissolve in excess ammonia (16.7a). Cr³⁺ gives a green precipitate; Zn²⁺ gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia.

blocks.prompt: IV. Addition of NH₄OH to an aqueous solution of a cation gives a green precipitate which turns brown upon standing. Which basic radical is indicated?
blocks.explanation: Fe²⁺ gives Fe(OH)₂, which is quickly oxidized by air to orange-brown Fe(OH)₃ (16.7f). Fe³⁺ gives a brown precipitate at once; Cr³⁺ gives a green precipitate that stays green; Cu²⁺ gives a blue one.

blocks.prompt: V. On dry heating test for salt analysis, the evolution of a colorless, odorless gas that turns limewater milky suggests the presence of:
blocks.explanation: The gas is CO₂: it turns lime water milky, Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O (16.6a). Many carbonates give CO₂ on heating, e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (beyond the chapter); nitrates give brown NO₂ instead.

blocks.prompt: VI. The chromyl chloride test is a specific confirmatory test for:
blocks.explanation: A chloride heated with K₂Cr₂O₇ and conc. H₂SO₄ gives orange-red vapours of chromyl chloride, CrO₂Cl₂; bromides and iodides do not form such a compound (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: VII. The brown ring test is a confirmatory test for which acid radical?
blocks.explanation: With freshly prepared FeSO₄ solution and conc. H₂SO₄ poured down the side, a nitrate gives a brown ring of [Fe(H₂O)₅NO]²⁺ where the two layers meet (beyond the chapter).

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. For which type of titration, methyl orange is used as an indicator?
blocks.explanation: Methyl orange (colour change about pH 3.1–4.4, red to yellow) is used for titrations of a strong acid with a weak base, e.g. HCl against NH₃(aq) or Na₂CO₃, where the equivalence point is acidic. It also works for strong acid–strong base (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: b. Explain why phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for the titration of a weak acid with a strong base but not for the titration of a strong acid with a weak base.
blocks.explanation:
Phenolphthalein changes colour at about pH 8–10.
Weak acid + strong base: the salt formed is basic, so the equivalence point is above 7 (about 8–9), inside this range; the colour change is sharp.
Strong acid + weak base: the salt is acidic, the equivalence point is below 7 (about 5); phenolphthalein would change colour long before or after it, giving a wrong end point. Methyl orange is used instead (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: c. Explain why different indicators change color over different pH ranges.
blocks.explanation: An indicator is a weak organic acid (or base), HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻, whose un-ionized form and ion have different colours. The colour changes when both forms are about equal, i.e. near pH = pKₐ of the indicator (about pKₐ ± 1). Each indicator has its own Kₐ, so each changes over its own pH range, e.g. methyl orange 3.1–4.4, phenolphthalein about 8–10 (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: d. It is always advisable to use dilute solutions while performing experiments in volumetric analysis? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation:
1. Accuracy: with dilute solutions a larger, easily measured volume is used, so the reading error (about ±0.05 cm³) is a small percentage, and one extra drop does not overshoot the end point.
2. Safety: dilute acids and bases are less corrosive and give less heat on mixing (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: e. White precipitates are formed when Ca²⁺, Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ all react separately with NaOH solution. How will you detect which basic radical is present?
blocks.explanation:
Add excess NaOH, then test a fresh portion with aqueous ammonia (in excess):
Ca²⁺: precipitate does not dissolve in excess NaOH; with NH₃ only slight turbidity or no precipitate.
Al³⁺: precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH (beyond the chapter); with NH₃ a white gelatinous precipitate insoluble in excess.
Zn²⁺: precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH; with NH₃ a white precipitate that dissolves in excess.

blocks.prompt: f. How Fe²⁺ can be distinguished from Fe³⁺ chemically?
blocks.explanation: Add NaOH (or aqueous ammonia) solution to each.

rows: Orange-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃ at once
Turns orange-brown on standing (oxidized by air)

blocks.prompt: g. Why Ca²⁺ does not give precipitate with aqueous ammonia?
blocks.explanation: Aqueous ammonia is a weak base: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ gives only a low OH⁻ concentration. Ca(OH)₂ is fairly soluble, so this small OH⁻ concentration is not enough to precipitate it; at most a slight turbidity appears (16.7c). Strong NaOH gives enough OH⁻ to precipitate Ca(OH)₂ (explanation beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: h. How will you find out the concentration of acetic acid in vinegar solution?
blocks.explanation:
By acid-base titration against a standard NaOH solution (method as in 16.5):
1. Dilute a measured volume of vinegar with distilled water (e.g. 10 times) and pipette a known volume (e.g. 10 cm³) into a conical flask.
2. Add 1–2 drops of phenolphthalein (weak acid–strong base).
3. Titrate with standard NaOH from the burette until a faint pink colour just persists; take concordant readings.
CH₃COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq) → CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l)
4. M₁V₁/n₁ (acid) = M₂V₂/n₂ (base), n₁ = n₂ = 1, gives the molarity of the diluted acid; multiply by the dilution factor. Concentration in g dm⁻³ = molarity × 60 g mol⁻¹ (molar mass of CH₃COOH).

blocks.prompt: i. What precautions you need to observe while diluting a concentrated acid?
blocks.explanation:
1. Always add the acid to water, slowly and in small portions with constant stirring; never add water to concentrated acid (the heat produced can boil the water and spatter acid).
2. Use a heat-resistant glass beaker, cooled in cold water if needed.
3. Wear a lab coat, safety goggles and gloves; work in a fume cupboard; never work alone (16.1).
(Details beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: j. Why does an aqueous solution of Na₂CO₃ behave like a base?
blocks.explanation:
Na₂CO₃ is a salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (H₂CO₃). In water the carbonate ion hydrolyses and produces OH⁻ ions:
CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
The excess OH⁻ makes the solution basic (pH above 7) (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: k. If an aqueous solution of NaOH is kept in an open container, what changes do you expect to take place with the passage of time?
blocks.explanation:
NaOH absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and is slowly converted into sodium carbonate:
2NaOH(aq) + CO₂(g) → Na₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
So the concentration of NaOH falls and the solution no longer has its labelled molarity; titration results become wrong (the chapter notes that atmospheric CO₂ interferes with the phenolphthalein end point). Water may also evaporate, changing the concentration.

blocks.prompt: Q.3 Describe common types of the Chemistry lab hazards with two examples in each case.
blocks.explanation:
Most lab hazards fall into three categories: physical, chemical and biological.
1. Physical hazards: dangers from the surroundings and equipment.
Examples: (i) slips and falls on a wet floor; (ii) cuts and abrasions from broken glassware.
Precautions: keep floors dry; wear cut-resistant gloves when handling broken glass and put it in a special container.
2. Chemical hazards: dangers from the chemicals themselves (corrosive, poisonous or inflammable).
Examples: (i) burns from concentrated acids and alkalis (e.g. H₂SO₄, NaOH) or bromine; (ii) fire from inflammable liquids such as spirit or oil, or poisoning by swallowing chemicals (e.g. salts of heavy metals).
Precautions: use chemicals by standard procedures; never taste or smell chemicals; wear lab coat and goggles; store and label waste properly.
3. Biological hazards: dangers from living organisms and their products.
Examples: (i) allergens; (ii) infectious diseases transferred from animals to humans, and viral diseases.
Precautions: no food in the lab; wear gloves; follow the warning signs.

rows: Slips and falls on a wet floor; cuts from broken glassware
Burns from concentrated acids, alkalis or bromine; fire from inflammable liquids (or poisoning)
Allergens; infectious diseases from animals to humans (and viral diseases)

blocks.prompt: Q.4 What are common accidents in the Chemistry lab? How they are managed in first aid treatment.
blocks.explanation:
Every laboratory must have a first aid box. Common accidents and first aid (Table 16.1):
1. Cuts: minor: remove any glass piece and apply methylated spirit or tincture of iodine on cotton (disinfectant). Serious: press on the cut for about 10 minutes to stop bleeding and consult a doctor.
2. Eye injuries: acid in the eye: wash with plenty of water, then 1% sodium bicarbonate solution. Alkali: water, then 1% boric acid solution. Foreign particle: do not rub; remove gently with a soft handkerchief and wash with water. Soreness: a drop of olive oil, keep the eyes closed for some time.
3. Burns: dry heat (flame, hot object): apply burnol or mustard oil. Acid burns: wash with ice-cold water, then saturated sodium bicarbonate solution, then water. Alkali burns: wash with water, then 1% acetic acid solution, then water; dry and apply burnol. Bromine burns: wash with 2% ammonia solution and apply glycerin, wipe it off later and apply burnol.
4. Poisons: swallowed poison: spit at once and rinse the mouth repeatedly. Acid swallowed: drink a lot of water, lime water or milk of magnesia. Caustic alkali swallowed: drink a lot of water and lemon or orange juice. Salts of heavy metals: take milk or egg white.
5. Fire: clothes on fire: do not run; wrap in a blanket or dry cotton cloth and lie on the floor. Beaker of inflammable liquid on fire: cover with a damp cloth to cut off oxygen. Spirit or oil fire: throw sand mixed with sodium bicarbonate, not water (water spreads it). Electrical fire: switch off the supply and throw sand, never water.
Any accident must be reported to the lab in-charge at once.

blocks.prompt:
Q.5 How the following acid radicals are indicated and confirmed in salt analysis:
i) CO₃²⁻ ii) Cl⁻ iii) NO₃⁻ iv) SO₄²⁻
blocks.explanation:
(The indicating tests are from the chapter, 16.6; the confirmatory tests are beyond the chapter.)
i) Carbonate, CO₃²⁻
Indicated: about 2 g of salt + 5 cm³ dilute HCl: brisk effervescence; the gas turns lime water milky.
CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l)
Confirmed: salt solution + MgSO₄ solution gives a white precipitate of MgCO₃ in the cold (a bicarbonate gives it only on boiling).
ii) Chloride, Cl⁻
Indicated: salt solution acidified with dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq): thick white precipitate of AgCl, soluble in aqueous NH₃.
Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
Confirmed (chromyl chloride test): heat the solid salt with solid K₂Cr₂O₇ and conc. H₂SO₄: orange-red vapours of CrO₂Cl₂. Passed into NaOH they give a yellow solution, which with acetic acid and lead acetate gives a yellow precipitate of PbCrO₄.
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 4Cl⁻ + 6H⁺ → 2CrO₂Cl₂ + 3H₂O
CrO₂Cl₂ + 4NaOH → Na₂CrO₄ + 2NaCl + 2H₂O
iii) Nitrate, NO₃⁻
Indicated: salt solution + NaOH solution + powdered aluminium, warm: smell of NH₃ gas, which turns moist red litmus blue. Aluminium is the reducing agent.
3NO₃⁻(aq) + 8Al(s) + 5OH⁻(aq) + 18H₂O(l) → 3NH₃(g) + 8[Al(OH)₄]⁻(aq)
Confirmed (brown ring test): to the salt solution add freshly prepared FeSO₄ solution, then pour conc. H₂SO₄ slowly down the side of the tube: a brown ring forms where the layers meet.
NO₃⁻ + 3Fe²⁺ + 4H⁺ → NO + 3Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O
[Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + NO → [Fe(H₂O)₅NO]²⁺ (brown) + H₂O
iv) Sulphate, SO₄²⁻
Indicated: salt solution acidified with dilute HNO₃ + barium nitrate solution: heavy white precipitate of BaSO₄ (the acid removes carbonate).
SO₄²⁻(aq) + Ba²⁺(aq) → BaSO₄(s)
Confirmed: the precipitate does not dissolve even in concentrated HCl or HNO₃; also, with lead acetate solution a white precipitate of PbSO₄ forms, which dissolves in ammonium acetate solution.

blocks.prompt:
Q.6 How the following basic radicals are indicated and confirmed in salt analysis:
i) Cu²⁺ ii) Al³⁺ iii) Fe³⁺ iv) Zn²⁺
blocks.explanation:
(Dissolve about 4 g of the salt in 10 cm³ distilled water and divide into portions. The NaOH and NH₃ tests are from the chapter, 16.7; the confirmatory tests and the reactions in excess reagent are beyond the chapter.)
i) Copper, Cu²⁺
Indicated: NaOH gives a light-blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂.
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)
Aqueous NH₃: a little gives a pale-blue precipitate; in excess it dissolves to a deep blue solution.
Cu(OH)₂(s) + 4NH₃(aq) → [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq)
Confirmed: potassium ferrocyanide, K₄[Fe(CN)₆], gives a chocolate-brown precipitate of Cu₂[Fe(CN)₆].
ii) Aluminium, Al³⁺
Indicated: NaOH gives a white gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)₃, which dissolves in excess NaOH; aqueous NH₃ gives a white precipitate insoluble in excess.
Al³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Al(OH)₃(s)
Al(OH)₃(s) + OH⁻(aq) → [Al(OH)₄]⁻(aq)
Confirmed (lake test): to the salt solution add two drops of blue litmus solution, then NH₄OH drop by drop: a blue precipitate (the 'lake', Al(OH)₃ that has adsorbed the dye) floats in a colourless solution.
iii) Iron(III), Fe³⁺
Indicated: NaOH or aqueous NH₃ gives an orange-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃ at once.
Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)
Confirmed: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] gives a deep (Prussian) blue precipitate, and potassium thiocyanate, KSCN, gives a blood-red colour.
4Fe³⁺ + 3[Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ → Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃
Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ → [Fe(SCN)]²⁺
iv) Zinc, Zn²⁺
Indicated: NaOH gives a white precipitate of Zn(OH)₂, soluble in excess NaOH; aqueous NH₃ gives a white precipitate, soluble in excess NH₃.
Zn²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Zn(OH)₂(s)
Zn(OH)₂(s) + 2OH⁻(aq) → [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻(aq)
Zn(OH)₂(s) + 4NH₃(aq) → [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq)
Confirmed: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] gives a white (bluish-white) precipitate.
